extracted.intended_audience: Employers, workplace safety managers, industry stakeholders, and commenters on OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for employer compliance with OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard (HIIPP), including what must be in written plans, monitoring options, employee involvement, and how OSHA estimated costs and labor rates for compliance. Useful for preparing comments or implementing the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-trigger dependent requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain requirements of the proposed standard are required only when the heat index meets or exceeds a specified heat trigger: the initial heat trigger at 80°F or the high heat trigger at 90°F. Requirements dependent on meeting/exceeding triggers include rest breaks (at both the initial and high heat triggers), acclimatization (at the initial heat trigger), effective communication (initial heat trigger), observation for signs and symptoms (high heat trigger), and Hazard Alert (high heat trigger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses these two heat-index thresholds to determine when specific protections apply; commenters may provide data on alternative triggers or thresholds. The analysis uses NOAA Local Climatological Data to estimate frequency by state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan (HIIPP) content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under paragraph (c) of the proposed standard, employers must create a written HIIPP that includes: a comprehensive list of the types of work activities covered by the plan; all policies and procedures necessary to comply with the requirements of this proposed standard including those to protect employees while wearing vapor-impermeable clothing; and identification of the heat metric (i.e., heat index or wet bulb globe temperature) the employer will monitor to identify heat hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may already have HIIPPs that need modification. OSHA expects use of templates will be common. Employers must designate personnel to implement the HIIPP and make the HIIPP available in languages employees understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of heat safety coordinator(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must designate one or more heat safety coordinators to implement and monitor the HIIPP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designated person(s) are the labor category used in OSHA's cost estimates; the designated person does not necessarily have to be a supervisor/manager even though wage derivation used supervisory/manager occupations as proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP availability and review cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must make the HIIPP readily available to all employees in a language that all employees understand, and must review the HIIPP whenever a heat-related incident occurs that results in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness. The review of the HIIPP must occur at least annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates one hour per year for designated person to review/update HIIPP; reviews triggered by qualifying incidents require reexamination. OSHA welcomes feedback on these timing assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee involvement in HIIPP development and updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must involve non-managerial employees in the creation or initial modification of the HIIPP and in the periodic review/update process. OSHA assumes a representative group of employees (four employees per establishment) will take one hour each during initial development to provide feedback and will take 20 minutes each during review/update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time for employee input is captured in cost estimates for HIIPP development and updates; OSHA seeks comments and data on these estimates and on how employers obtain employee input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for HIIPP development and associated time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may (a) write a HIIPP from scratch (OSHA estimates ~30 hours for designated person), (b) use a HIIPP template (estimated ~6 hours for designated person), or (c) employers with ten or fewer employees (exempt from writing HIIPP) may spend ~4 hours using a template to guide creation. OSHA assumes 5% of employers will have complex/unique situations requiring ~30 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA expects most employers will use templates rather than drafting from scratch. The agency requests information on actual employer experience and time spent developing HIIPPs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule familiarization requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All employers affected by the proposed standard must review the requirements; OSHA estimates rule familiarization will take a designated person one hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many employers will rely on compliance assistance documents from OSHA or trade associations, which OSHA assumes will reduce familiarization time compared to reading regulatory text directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring requirement for outdoor worksites (methods and time assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For outdoor worksites, employers must monitor heat conditions using either local heat index forecasts or on-site measurement of heat index or WBGT. OSHA assumes employers without current monitoring will use local forecasts and that, on average, a designated person will take approximately 15 seconds twice a day to monitor the local forecast via a smartphone app.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively employers may set up on-site monitoring (measure heat index or WBGT). OSHA's cost analysis assumes the low-effort forecast-monitoring approach will be preferred for new adopters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring requirement for indoor worksites and hazard evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoor employers must conduct a hazard evaluation to identify work areas where there is a reasonable expectation that employees are or may be exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger; OSHA estimates the hazard evaluation will require about 3 hours in total. Indoor employers do not have the option to rely on local weather forecasts and instead must use on-site measurements (heat index or WBGT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must seek input of non-managerial employees when evaluating worksites; OSHA assumes four employees per establishment provide input at 15 minutes each. Employers may elect to forgo measurements by assuming an area meets/exceeds both triggers, but then must comply with all required controls for both triggers (OSHA assumes none will newly adopt this option because of cost tradeoffs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed monitoring metrics and tools (heat index vs WBGT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may measure the heat index (from ambient temperature and humidity, possibly using OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App or NWS online calculator) or measure wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) using WBGT thermometers. Employers may set up temperature and humidity loggers capable of automatically uploading data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates measuring heat index takes ~1 minute each time (twice/day) and reading a logger manual takes ~15 minutes. OSHA assumes no employers will newly adopt WBGT measurements (though employers already using WBGT may continue without additional estimated costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring frequency and recordkeeping assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA assumes measurements (for on-site heat index monitoring) will be taken twice per work day (260 days per year) and that devices (e.g., loggers) will be capable of automatic uploads for recordkeeping. Designated person initial setup time (e.g., reading logger manual) is estimated at ~15 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are modelling assumptions for cost estimation; OSHA welcomes data to refine monitoring frequency and setup time assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer option to assume area meets/exceeds triggers (no measurements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard allows employers to forgo taking measurements if they assume that a work area meets or exceeds both heat triggers. Employers electing to do this would not incur monitoring costs but would be required to comply with all control measures required at both triggers as though measurements met/exceeded the high trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes no employers will newly adopt this option because implementing controls for both triggers is typically more expensive than monitoring; requests comment on types of employers that might choose this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor classification and wage derivation methodology (designated person vs at-risk worker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two employee types are used in cost estimates: 'designated person' and 'at-risk worker.' Designated person wages were derived by filtering OEWS data for occupations that included 'Manager,' 'Supervisor,' or 'Director' and calculating weighted average hourly wages per sector; at-risk worker wages were calculated using OEWS data at the 2-digit NAICS sector level with occupation shares and median wages to compute sector-weighted averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes this method may overestimate designated person wages because the designated person need not be a manager; the agency invites feedback on wage assumptions and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loaded hourly wage calculation and cost components
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate fully loaded hourly labor cost, OSHA adds base wages + fringe benefits + applicable overhead. Fringe benefits are estimated as 45 percent of base wages (31.1 percent of total compensation). Overhead is estimated as 17 percent of base wages (equivalent to 11.71 percent of the hourly wage rate with fringe applied). The formula used: loaded hourly wage = median hourly wage * (1 + fringe rate) * (1 + fringe-adjusted overhead rate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 17% overhead rate is drawn from EPA (2002) and Rice (2002) and is used for safety and health professionals in large private organizations; OSHA acknowledges it may be an overestimate for this context and requests comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for estimating heat-related illnesses and risk reduction effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA's illness estimates apply an undercount factor of 7.5 for non-fatal heat-related illnesses and 3 for fatal heat-related illnesses (based on BLS data), assumes an effectiveness rate of 95 percent in reducing heat-related fatal illnesses and 65 percent for non-fatal illnesses, and assumes 5.3 percent of heat-related illnesses are emergencies (the rest are non-emergencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions are used to estimate average expected annual numbers of heat-related illnesses by industry sector and per-establishment incidence rates; OSHA explicitly welcomes feedback on these data and methods and notes possible variability in underreporting across sectors/occupations.
